assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with laser-cooled trapped ions turned the ion trap into a concrete quantum-computing architecture, and Blatt's group and others realised entangling gates, teleportation and multi-qubit algorithms with record fidelities. The discovery is original, conceptually clean and has shaped the whole field of quantum information hardware, including the analogue simulation programme.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the decisive 1995 theoretical proposal and Blatt is the leading experimental realiser of the scheme; the three-name configuration is coherent. Wineland's 2012 prize covered ion control and spectroscopy, and other experimental leaders such as Monroe and Wineland's group overlap with this story but are not in the credited names, which is a fairness question.
assessment.maturity: Mature: three decades of independent confirmation across many laboratories and now commercial machines. Timing is good, although overlap with the 2012 prize and the open race among qubit platforms could make the committee cautious.
uncertainties: Overlap in scope with the 2012 trapped-ion prize and a possible argument that Cirac and Zoller are better rewarded for broader contributions across AMO quantum information.
Whether Monroe and others who demonstrated the first gate should be credited is not resolved by the supplied names; I am relying on my own recollection of the history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED made it possible to couple a superconducting artificial atom strongly to a single microwave photon in a resonator, giving dispersive readout, quantum buses and the dominant architecture for superconducting processors. This is a field I know closely and it is both original and extremely influential beyond quantum computing, in microwave quantum optics.
assessment.attribution: The 2004 proposal is by Blais, Huang, Wallraff, Girvin and Schoelkopf and the first experiment by Wallraff et al. in Schoelkopf's group. Three names cannot cover Girvin's theory role, which is an unresolved allocation, and I would flag it openly. I propose Blais for theory, Wallraff and Schoelkopf for the experiments.
assessment.maturity: Very mature and independently confirmed in many groups. The 2025 prize recognised macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in circuits, so the committee may feel the circuit field has just been honoured, and I declare my own professional proximity to this subfield as a limit on my neutrality.
uncertainties: Conflict between recency of the 2025 prize and the distinct scientific content of cQED.
Girvin's exclusion from a three-person limit is a credit dispute that could be seen as unfair.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error correction and fault tolerance underpin the whole claim that large quantum computers are possible. Shor's code, Steane's codes and Kitaev's toric code and anyonic fault tolerance are original and fundamental, and the threshold theorem changed the status of quantum computing from an idea to an engineering problem.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane independently introduced the first quantum codes in 1995-96 and Kitaev introduced topological codes and fault tolerance. Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme, Aharonov and Ben-Or and others also made decisive contributions, so any three-person configuration is partial and contentious.
assessment.maturity: Theory is well established and now meeting experiments with below-threshold surface-code memories, but a fully fault-tolerant machine does not exist yet, so recognition may be seen as slightly early. It is also mathematical in flavour, and the committee may weigh its physical discovery content.
uncertainties: Whether the discovery is physics or information theory in the committee's view.
Many other contributors, especially Gottesman, Calderbank, Knill and Laflamme, and unclear boundary of the 'compound' topic.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18, using Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's realisation with strontium. They reshaped precision measurement, enabling tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a possible redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: A clean two-person credit: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and Ye's group delivered the record accuracy and stability. Other clock groups (ion clocks, Lemke, Ludlow and others) contributed but the supplied names fit a fair prize.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent clocks and mature. Timing is good, though the redefinition of the second has not yet happened and Hall and Hänsch (2005) and Wineland (2012) have already been honoured for related techniques.
uncertainties: Proximity to prior prizes for frequency combs and ion clocks.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the redefinition of the second.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical prediction of flat bands at the magic angle and the 2018 discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene opened moiré quantum materials as a whole new platform for strongly correlated and topological physics. It is highly original with a vast, fast-growing literature.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the 2011 theoretical prediction and Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery. Cao, the first author of the experiments, and the Dean and Young groups, plus Efetov and others, also contributed, so the allocation is not fully resolved. A three-name prize with a theorist pair and one experimentalist is plausible.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and the interpretation of the superconducting mechanism is still unsettled. The phenomenon is solid, but the field is young, so it is perhaps slightly premature relative to the older candidates.
uncertainties: Credit to student first authors and to other moiré groups beyond the three names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of the quantum spin Hall state in graphene and then the topological insulator classification, together with the observation in HgTe quantum wells, created the field of time-reversal-invariant topological matter. It is a deep and lasting conceptual advance with many experimental realisations.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical proposals; Molenkamp's group observed the quantum spin Hall edge transport in HgTe following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (deceased) and Hasan's early ARPES work are not all representable, so credit is complicated. I use only Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, leaving Hasan and others out of this particular configuration.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many material systems for fifteen years, though application remains modest. The topology theme was recognised in 2016 (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz), which a committee may weigh.
uncertainties: Omission of Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan makes any prize arguably unfair.
Overlap with the 2016 topological prize in the committee's view.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond created a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a very versatile nanoscale quantum sensor, with uses from magnetometry to biological sensing. The impact is wide and the work is original and experimentally clean.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the first single-NV optical detection and spin control; Lukin's group contributed key quantum-information and sensing demonstrations with Walsworth, Awschalom, Hanson, Budker and others. The credit allocation to Lukin versus others is an open question that I flag.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many groups; sensing applications continue to be developed. The timing is reasonable but practical impact beyond research tools is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with candidates on optically addressed spin qubits and the fair share of Awschalom, Hanson and Imamoglu.
Whether sensing or qubit aspects is the central discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The 1988 observation of quantised conductance in quantum point contacts was a founding experiment of mesoscopic transport, showing Landauer-type ballistic conductance steps in a semiconductor heterostructure. It remains a textbook result and a building block of gate-defined quantum devices and spin and Majorana platforms. It sits in a field I know well.
assessment.attribution: Two groups made the discovery simultaneously, the Delft-Philips group of van Wees, van Houten and colleagues and the Cambridge group of Wharam, Thornton, Pepper and colleagues. The supplied names omit Wharam and Thornton, so the distribution of credit among the experimentalists, and the theoretical credit to Landauer and Büttiker (both deceased), are not fully resolved.
assessment.maturity: Over thirty years old and entirely confirmed, so there is no maturity risk; the question is whether recognition is now overdue and whether the committee regards it as a Nobel-level conceptual discovery rather than a landmark technical demonstration.
uncertainties: Overlap with the Nobel-recognised integer quantum Hall effect.
Attribution among the two groups and the omission of the Cambridge co-authors.
